extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Canadian history; historians of policing; readers interested in the North-West Mounted Police
extracted.subtask_description: A historical account describing the founding, recruitment, organization, character and early operations of the North-West (Canadian) Mounted Police in the late 19th century. Focuses on the qualities desired in recruits, organizational design choices, and the force's role in settling and policing the West.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory enlistment eligibility clause
rubrics_metrics.description: "No person shall be appointed to the police force unless he be of sound constitution, able to ride, active and able-bodied, and between the ages of eighteen and forty years, nor unless he be able to read and write either the English or the French language."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause from the Act was applied in practice because recruits would patrol the widest and wildest frontier; literacy in either official language and physical fitness were required for operational effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobility of force (not fixed forts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Butler advocated a material force which would be located "not at fixed points or forts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: fixed points would "afford little protection outside the immediate circle of these points and would hold out no inducements to the establishment of new settlements." A movable force was necessary to respond to scattered settlements and to encourage settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and factional independence (non-partisanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a force should be independent of any faction or party either in church or state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and historical practice: Mounted Police remained strictly non-partisan, resisted political interference, and treated everyone alike "regardless of race or creed or colour," contributing to reputation for even-handed justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil (not military) character of the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: This was to be a civil force in uniform, not a military organization subject to the Queen's regulations, but dependent for discipline upon the personality of the officers, the esprit de corps... and the noblesse oblige idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: discipline should rely on officer leadership, esprit de corps and internal standards rather than formal military code; the force should emphasize hardiness and readiness over ceremonial 'fuss and feathers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform as instrument of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The red coat was the visible and definite assurance that right was might. A red speck on the horizon was notice... that the rule of law prevailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: use of bright scarlet colour had moral/psychological effect—disconcerts ill-affected, associates the force with regular troops and law, and visibly signals authority and deterrence to both settlers and Indigenous peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and personal qualities of recruits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruits should be of sound constitution, able to ride, active and able-bodied... good physique and respectable character; genuine manhood was the only hall-mark allowed as a standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanded desirable traits mentioned: endurance, initiative, reliability, courage, powers of observation, forecasting ability, willingness to share perils, leadership by example. The force weeded out misfits and moral/physical undesirables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literacy requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor unless he be able to read and write either the English or the French language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: clerical/administrative duties, following orders, reporting and communication across a vast frontier required basic literacy in one of the official languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection / enlistment process should sift out undesirables
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of enlistment was hurried somewhat and later on some sifting was done in order to throw out any culls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance: despite recruitment pressures, leadership (e.g., Commissioner French) took steps to weed out undesirables, warned recruits about hardships to discourage the faint-hearted, and maintained standards over time to preserve corps' reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership by example and esprit de corps
rubrics_metrics.description: "I know of no officer in the force who would order any man to do any work at all, that the officer would not do himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: officer conduct and willingness to share danger/work builds men’s confidence, produces strong internal discipline, and fosters a culture eliminating social distinctions—leadership personality rather than formal coercion maintained order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational mission: protect settlers and secure development
rubrics_metrics.description: The force was to be a protector and guide to the settlers who would flow into the West... settlers did not hesitate to go where there was Mounted Police protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions enumerated: establish constituted authority, provide security for life and property, suppress robbery and murder, control liquor traffic, support orderly settlement, assist families and homesteaders, patrol remote areas to promote development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Indigenous populations with restraint and mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: The first business our Mounted Police did was to stand between the Indians and the vile creatures who would give them drink and rob them of all they possessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: police role included protecting Indigenous communities from exploiters/outlaw traders, mediating and controlling intertribal violence where possible, and preventing large-scale military conflict—aimed at peaceful relations rather than antagonism.
